cards.f: Costovertebral angle (CVA) tenderness — What you are looking for?
cards.b: Tenderness at the angle between the 12th rib and the vertebral column — localises the problem to the kidney

cards.f: Sudden onset, severity 10/10 — What it tells you?
cards.b: Classic for acute ureteric obstruction by a stone

cards.b: Argues against musculoskeletal / radicular pain, which changes with movement

cards.f: No urinary symptoms — What it tells you?
No GI symptoms — What it tells you?
cards.b: Bowel causes (appendicitis, obstruction, diverticulitis) less likely

cards.b: Raised WBC = infection → changes management (see Stage 2)
Renal impairment is an indication to intervene
Haematuria supports a stone; pyuria/nitrites suggest infection (send culture)
Cheap, quick, low dose; good for follow-up of a known radio-opaque stone
Misses radiolucent stones (uric acid, xanthine); bowel gas and bone overlap
No radiation — first choice in pregnancy and children
Poor at seeing ureteric stones; operator dependent
Contrast excretion → level of obstruction, delayed function
IV contrast (allergy, nephrotoxicity), radiation, slow — largely replaced by CT
Dilated collecting system; stone seen as a filling defect
Stones themselves poorly seen; costly, less available
Most sensitive and specific; detects alternative diagnoses

cards.b: Retrograde — cystoscopy, up the ureter past the stone
Percutaneous — needle and tube through the flank into the renal pelvis (US / fluoroscopy guided)
Internal; proximal curl in the kidney, distal curl in the bladder
Tube from renal pelvis exits the skin
External, into a bag (output can be measured)
No external bag; comfortable once settled
Does not need to pass the stone; useful when retrograde access fails
Stent symptoms (frequency, urgency, haematuria, flank pain on voiding); must be removed / changed later

cards.f: ESWL extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy — How it works?
cards.b: Shock waves generated outside the body are focused on the stone (located by X-ray / US); fragments then pass in the urine
Scope passed via urethra and bladder up the ureter; stone fragmented (laser) and/or removed (basket). A flexible scope reaches stones inside the kidney
Tract made from the flank directly into the kidney; stone fragmented and extracted
Cystoscope via the urethra; bladder stone crushed / fragmented and washed out
